questions.q: What are the three main elements of voice that change when reading a story aloud?
questions.a: The three elements are pace, volume, and expression (or tone). If a student answers only "reading fast," it reveals they are missing the importance of volume and expression in creating a mood.

questions.q: If a character in a story is running in a race, how should your reading speed change compared to when they are standing still and thinking?
questions.a: Your speed should increase during the race and slow down during the thinking part. A wrong answer suggests the student treats all sentences with the same "flat" rhythm, failing to see the connection between action and pace.

questions.q: When you read a line like "Prabhat felt terrible about losing," how can you use your face or body to dramatise this without adding new words?
questions.a: You could slump your shoulders and look down while reading the line to show sadness. A wrong answer (like jumping around) shows a failure to link physical movement to the specific emotion of the text.

questions.q: Compare how you would read a sentence about someone "whispering a secret" versus "shouting for help." What changes?
questions.a: You would lower your volume and slow down for the secret, but increase volume and pitch for the shout. If a student keeps the same volume for both, they are not using "vocal variety" to signal meaning.

questions.q: Why is it better to slow down during a suspenseful part of a story rather than reading through it as quickly as possible?
questions.a: Slowing down builds anticipation and allows the listener to feel the tension. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks reading is only about finishing the words, not about the effect on the audience.

questions.q: Create a short action sentence for a character who is happy about winning a game, and describe how you would say it out loud.
questions.a: Example: "I finally did it!" with a bright, energetic tone and a wide smile. A poor answer would just be a sentence without any description of the performance, failing to demonstrate the "dramatisation" part of the task.
